title: Downfall
full_review:
History's most infamous dictator, Adolf Hitler, has been fodder for many a Hollywood and British production over the years, but "Downfall" (Newmarket) is reportedly the first German theatrical film to deal with Hitler since the 1956 G.W. Pabst film, "Der Letste Akt" ("The Last Act"), which told the story of the Fuhrer's final days from the limited viewpoint of an ordinary soldier.

Oliver Hirshbiegel's film, an Academy Award nominee in the Foreign Film category, is a vividly authentic recreation of that same 1945 period during which Hitler (Bruno Ganz) was trapped in his Berlin-based underground hideout as the Russian army closed in for certain victory at the end of World War II.

The bunker was no small shack, but a complex of rooms where life, including elegantly served meals, and military strategizing was conducted in remarkably business-as-usual fashion.

Other famous names from the Third Reich share the claustrophobic bunker space, too -- Heinrich Himmler (Ulrich Noethen), Hermann Fegelein (Thomas Kretschmann), Joseph Goebbels (Ulrich Matthes), Albert Speer (Heino Ferch) -- some, like Goebbels, with their families.

As Hitler increasingly loses his reason, he comes to believe they will somehow be liberated, and he and his staff pore over maps looking in vain for salvation. When he finally realizes they are fighting a losing battle, he lashes out at what he perceives as his cowardly commanders, calling them "scum." He expresses the hope that the city be destroyed before the Russians take over.

He demands total obedience, even though the end is clearly near. When he hears that his mistress Eva Braun's brother-in-law, Fegelein, has left the bunker, he insists that he be found and shot. Eva (Juliane Kohler) pleads for his life, but ultimately goes along with her consort's wishes. The man is dragged out of a nearby brothel -- there are some brief shots of decadent cavorting -- and summarily executed.

Rest assured, this is no glorification of Hitler. At one point, we see him reveling in the fact that he's "cleared the land of Jewish poison."

There are parallel stories, one involving a boy, Peter, who is part of the Hitler Youth movement, and despite protestations from his father, perseveres as a street fighter.

And there's the dedicated Professor Schenck (Christian Berkel), who joins professor Werner Haase (Matthias Habich) in ministering to the sick and horribly wounded. (Be warned: There are several fleeting, but gruesome, scenes of limbs being sawed off.) The bombing and fighting scenes are quite intense, but the film doesn't wallow in its violence; what violence there is certainly reinforces the horrific nature of war, particularly on innocent civilians.

As the Russian troops move ever closer, Hitler and the others plan how best to commit suicide, placing "honor" above all else. He and Eva (whom he marries in the bunker, after dictating his testament) will take poison and shoot themselves at the same time. Hitler asks Otto Gunsche (Gotz Otto) to be sure to burn their bodies so they won't be put on display by the victors.

All this is seen through the eyes of Traudl Junge (Alexandra Maria Lara), his young personal secretary. Indeed, the film was based partly on her book "Until the Final Hour: Hitler's Last Secretary" (written with Melissa Muller). The other source was "Inside Hitler's Bunker: The Last Days of the Third Reich" by Joachim Fest.

Traudl stayed with him through his suicide, eventually managing to escape through enemy lines. The real Traudl -- who died in 2002 and was the subject of the documentary "Blind Spot: Hitler's Secretary" -- appears in a postscript at the end of the film, admitting that her youth was no excuse for ignorance of Hitler's heinous acts.

The German-language film has impeccable production values, and you have a real "you are there" feeling.

The performances are first rate. Ganz, who carefully studied Hitler's voice, impersonates him flawlessly: one minute, an almost kindly middle-aged man, the next a raving, paranoid and delusional maniac. (Traudl can't understand how Hitler can be so caring and then so brutal, and Ganz conveys this mercurial temperament.) Kohler seems to be walking the line between sanity and hysteria as Eva's party-girl persona morphs into grim realization of her fate.

Corinna Harfouch as Magda Goebbels is quite chilling in her hysteria and then her steely resolve to kill her children to protect them from the horrors to come. In one of the film's most devastating scenes, she has each of them drink a sleeping potion, and then creeps in later to put cyanide capsules in their mouths one by one. Afterward, her husband takes her outside, shooting her and then himself. And all because she can't imagine living without National Socialism!

Lara projects a sweet sincerity in her dedication to the man she feels it's her honor to serve, without perhaps understanding the enormity of his crimes, and a growing disbelief of her situation.

The film generates a good deal of suspense even though the historical outcome is known. There's also a real fascination in having this story told in a German production. As with the World War I submarine drama, "Das Boot," it's instructive to observe the war from the other side's perspective.

Subtitles.

The film contains some crude language, multiple suicides and wartime violence, some with attendant gore, brief but brutal scenes of amputation, partial nudity, a brief sexual situation, heavy smoking and alcohol use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
